title: Upasiva's question
hook: one of the sixteen asks what to rely on to cross; the Buddha answers, nothingness, mindfully

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Parayana, sixteen students walking north to ask their questions. Your line: crossing the flood. Today, one of the sixteen asks his.

Upasiva is the sixth of the sixteen to speak. His question is short, and plain. Alone, he says, with nothing to hold on to, I can't cross the great flood. Tell me something to lean on. It's a sentence that could be said at the edge of anything too big: a diagnosis, a debt, a loss. Not what is the meaning of life. Just: what do I hold?
screen: `THE SIXTH OF THE SIXTEEN.` → `ALONE, I CAN'T CROSS.` → `TELL ME SOMETHING TO LEAN ON.`

segments.voice: The Buddha's answer is surprising. Mindful, he says, looking to nothingness, leaning on the thought there is nothing, cross the flood. Let go of sense-desires, step back from talk, and watch, day and night, for the end of craving. Upasiva had meditated deeply; the commentary says he already knew the meditation called the base of nothingness. So the Buddha meets him there, in the place he already knows, and adds the one thing that turns it from a resting place into a crossing: mindfulness. Upasiva asks more. If someone stays there, would he become cool and freed right there, or would his consciousness pass on? The Buddha gives an image. As a flame blown out by the wind goes to rest and can't be counted any more, so the sage, freed, goes to rest and can't be counted. Does he not exist then, Upasiva asks, or is he forever well? There's no measuring the one who has gone to rest, the Buddha says. When everything is uprooted, every way of speaking about him is uprooted too. That last answer refuses both easy options. And with it, this path leaves the Sutta Nipata: from the snake shedding its skin, through the herdsman in the rain, the rhinoceros, the jewel, the blessings, the poet, the dart, the eights, all the way to this crossing. Tomorrow, a new book, of joy.
screen: `MINDFUL, LOOKING TO NOTHINGNESS.` · `MEETING HIM WHERE HE IS.` · `A FLAME BLOWN OUT BY THE WIND.` · `NO MEASURING THE ONE AT REST.` · then, large: `MINDFUL, CROSS.`

segments.voice: Notice what you usually lean on when things get hard: your phone, a plan, someone's reassurance; you don't have to give any of them up. For now, lean on nothing but knowing what's happening: breath in, known; breath out, known; a sound, known. When the mind reaches for a handhold, notice the reaching, and come back.
Upasiva's question. One of the sixteen asks what to lean on to cross the flood, and is told: mindful, looking to nothingness, cross.
Your line: mindful, cross. One step, fully known, is a place to start. Day six hundred ten, done.

howItsDone: Teachers often cite Upasiva's question when explaining nibbana as the flame gone out, and the image of the flame that can no longer be reckoned is common in Theravada teaching on what can and cannot be said of the awakened.

fork.setup: Upasiva asks: is the freed one gone, or forever well? what does the Buddha say?
options: there's no measuring him; the ways of speaking are uprooted.
fork.reveal: he refuses both options. like a flame gone out, the freed one can't be counted in the old terms.

original.note: Pali ogha: a flood. crossing the ogha is the image that runs through the Parayana.

trapdoor: what you thought: nirvana means being snuffed out.
what it means: in Sn 5.7 the flame gone out can't be measured; neither 'he is not' nor 'he is forever' fits.
what a scholar hears: Sn 5.7 uses the fire simile (accī yathā vātavegena khittā) for the arahant who can't be reckoned (na upeti sankham).

chat.says: When Upasiva asked what to lean on, what did the Buddha tell him?
options: Be mindful, looking to nothingness, and cross the flood.
Lean on your teacher Bavari; he'll carry you over the flood.
Hold tight to your own willpower, and push across alone.
chat.meaning: The Buddha meets Upasiva in the meditation he already knows and adds mindfulness, which turns a resting place into a crossing.

base of nothingness.meaning: a deep meditation that rests on the thought there is nothing

commentary.meaning: a later explanation of an old text

Sutta Nipata.meaning: a small, old collection of mostly verse discourses

notes: Sn 5.7 paraphrased. Confirm the order of Upasiva's three questions and the flame simile.
That Upasiva already knew the base of nothingness comes from the commentary (Niddesa / Paramatthajotika); confirm.
Readings differ on 'looking to nothingness' (akincanna): as the formless attainment used as a support, or more broadly as 'nothing' to hold. The script follows the commentary's reading.
This day closes the Sutta Nipata section (days 576–610) and points to the Udana.

Editor review (2026-10-01): SERIOUS fix: the teach rendered Upasiva's second question as 'does he go cold, or is he freed?', setting 'cool' against 'freed'; in Sn 1073 'cool' (siti) means liberated, and the alternative is whether his consciousness passes on. Also cut the superlatives 'the most honest thing anyone says in the whole chapter' and 'famous', the 'anyone who has stood... knows' line, and corrected the trapdoor Pali to khitta (agreeing with acci). The path leaves the Sutta Nipata here, but the Parayana goes on for ten more questions, so 'close the Sutta Nipata' became 'close our time in'.
